claim: METR (Kwa et al.) define the 50%-task-completion time horizon as the human-expert time of tasks a model completes with 50% success; on RE-Bench+HCAST+SWAA, Claude 3.7 Sonnet (Feb 2025) had a p50 horizon of about 50 minutes and the frontier p50 horizon doubled roughly every 7 months 2019-2025, possibly faster in 2024.
quote: On these tasks, current frontier AI models such as Claude 3.7 Sonnet have a 50% time horizon of around 50 minutes. Furthermore, frontier AI time horizon has been doubling approximately every seven months since 2019, though the trend may have accelerated in 2024.
source: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (arXiv 2503.14499; v4 retitled 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks')
by: Thomas Kwa, Ben West et al. (METR)

claim: In the original METR study the 80% horizon doubled at the same rate as the 50% horizon (213 vs 212 days) but horizons were roughly 5x shorter overall; Claude 3.7 Sonnet had the longest p80 horizon (~15 min) vs its p50 of 59 min (about 4x); METR reads the gap as models not reliably doing moderate-length tasks even when they sometimes succeed at hard ones.
original_claim: In the original METR study the 80% horizon doubled at the same rate as the 50% horizon (213 vs 212 days) but was about 4x shorter: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, the best model, had a p80 horizon of ~15 min vs a p50 of 59 min; METR reads this as models not reliably doing moderate-length tasks even when they sometimes succeed at hard ones.
quote: However, there is a large gap between models’ 50% time horizon and 80% time horizon—Claude 3.7 Sonnet has the longest 80%-horizon among models we examined at around 15 minutes, in contrast to its 50%-horizon of 59 minutes. This gap suggests that even models that sometimes succeed on difficult and diverse tasks cannot reliably perform tasks of moderate length.
source: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (arXiv 2503.14499; v4 retitled 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks')
by: Thomas Kwa, Ben West et al. (METR)

claim: Controlling for task length, each extra point of METR's 16-factor 'messiness' score (resource limits, novelty, dynamic environment, real-world sourcing, etc.) cut mean agent success by roughly 8.1% on HCAST/RE-Bench tasks (whose mean messiness was only 3.2/16, none above 8); the improvement trend over time was similar for messy and clean tasks.
quote: An increase in task messiness by 1 point reduces mean success rates by roughly 8.1%
source: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (arXiv 2503.14499; v4 retitled 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks')
by: Thomas Kwa, Ben West et al. (METR)

claim: METR's qualitative analysis: agents (early 2025) still struggle in 'messier' environments, specifically those without clear feedback loops or where the agent must proactively seek out relevant information; i.e. tasks with built-in checks and supplied context suit agents better.
quote: However, we noticed that AI agents still seem to struggle in intuitively “messier” environments—specifically, environments without clear feedback loops, or where the agent needs to proactively seek out relevant information.
source: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (arXiv 2503.14499; v4 retitled 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks')
by: Thomas Kwa, Ben West et al. (METR)

claim: On five real issues from an internal METR repo (run with GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) and o1), contract baseliners took 5x-18x longer than the repository maintainers, which METR says suggests time horizons may correspond better to the labor of a low-context human than a high-context one.
original_claim: On five real issues from an internal METR repo, contract baseliners took 5x-18x longer than the repository maintainers, so METR concludes time horizons correspond to the labor of a low-context human (new hire/contractor) rather than a high-context maintainer; an agent's horizon in maintainer-hours on a familiar repo is correspondingly much smaller.
quote: We find that our contract baseliners take 5x-18x longer to resolve issues than repository maintainers. … This suggests that time horizons may have better correspondence to the labor of a low-context human, rather than a high-context human.
source: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (arXiv 2503.14499; v4 retitled 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks')
by: Thomas Kwa, Ben West et al. (METR)

claim: METR Time Horizon 1.1 (228 tasks, 31 of them 8h+, Inspect infrastructure): post-2023 p50 doubling time 131 days (vs 165 under TH1), post-2024 89 days (vs 109); the post's re-estimated p50 horizons include Claude Opus 4.5 320 min [170,729], GPT-5 214 min, o3 121 min (the live dashboard later lists Opus 4.5 at 293 min and GPT-5 at 203 min); only 5 of the 31 long tasks have measured human baselines and METR says the suite is nearing saturation.
quote: The post-2023 doubling-time is 131 days under TH1.1, compared to 165 days under TH1, meaning progress is estimated to be 20% more rapid under TH1.1.
source: Time Horizon 1.1

claim: METR's live time-horizons page (last updated 2026-05-08, TH1.1, units minutes) lists the newest frontier value as Claude Mythos Preview (early, released 2026-04-07): p50 ~1045 min (~17.4 h, 95% CI 509-3304 min) but p80 only ~186 min (~3.1 h, CI 97-399 min), a ~5.6x p50/p80 gap; the p50 exceeds the 16-hour ceiling METR says its suite can measure.
quote: "claude_mythos_preview_early_inspect":{"benchmark_name":"METR-Horizon-v1.1","metrics":{"average_score":{"estimate":0.85205},"is_sota":true,"p50_horizon_length":{"ci_high":3304.261235,"ci_low":508.876789,"estimate":1044.780145},"p80_horizon_length":{"ci_high":398.514614,"ci_low":97.30292,"estimate":185.911829}}
source: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models (embedded benchmarkDataV1_1)

claim: On the same page, Claude Opus 4.6 (2026-02-05) has p50 ~719 min (~12 h, CI 317-3634) but p80 ~70 min (CI 27-170), a ~10x gap; other early-2026 models show 4-6x gaps (GPT-5.4 p50 342 / p80 54 min; Gemini 3.1 Pro 384 / 90; GPT-5.3 Codex 350 / 55). The 80%-reliable task length of 2026 frontier models is on the order of 1-3 human-hours even when p50 is 6-17 hours.
quote: "claude_opus_4_6_inspect":{"benchmark_name":"METR-Horizon-v1.1","metrics":{"average_score":{"estimate":0.788644},"is_sota":true,"p50_horizon_length":{"ci_high":3633.786163,"ci_low":316.685725,"estimate":718.80683},"p80_horizon_length":{"ci_high":170.437873,"ci_low":27.026521,"estimate":69.874587}}
source: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models (embedded benchmarkDataV1_1)

claim: METR states its current suite cannot measure horizons above 16 hours reliably, and that its task durations reflect low-context humans on self-contained, well-specified tasks; a '2-hour task' is what a new hire or freelance contractor could do in 2 hours, not an experienced project member.
quote: We think it’s better to think of our 2-hour tasks as what someone with low or no prior context (like a new hire or freelance contractor) could complete in 2 hours, rather than someone experienced who is already familiar with the project.
source: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models (FAQ)

claim: METR: time horizon is task difficulty in human-expert time, not how long the agent runs; agents are typically several times faster than humans on tasks they complete, partly because they take fewer actions.
quote: It’s a measure of the difficulty of a task, rather than the time an AI spends to complete the task. How long do AI agents take to complete a 2-hour task? It varies by model, task, and the exact agent setup, but AI agents are typically several times faster than humans on tasks they complete successfully.
source: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models (FAQ)

claim: METR's lead author warns against sizing delegated work by the p50 horizon: a 50% horizon of X hours does not mean tasks under X hours can be delegated, because reliability-critical, poorly verifiable tasks need 98%+ success to be worth automating.
quote: A 50% time horizon of X hours does not mean we can delegate tasks under X hours to AIs. Some (reliability-critical and poorly verifiable) tasks require 98%+ success probabilities to be worth automating
source: Clarifying limitations of time horizon

claim: Kwa (METR): doubling the horizon does not double automation; fewer interventions may each cost more human labor because failures get more complex, so human review cost per task must be measured separately (prompting, waiting, checking output).
quote: Doubling the time horizon does not double the degree of automation. Even if the AI requires half as many human interventions, it will probably fail in more complex ways requiring more human labor per intervention.
source: Clarifying limitations of time horizon

claim: Kwa (METR): horizon error bars are historically ~2x in each direction and worse near saturation (Opus 4.5), and the 80% horizon is not an independent estimate but comes from the same 2-parameter logistic fit, so improving on hard tasks can even lower the p80; 99% horizons would need ~300 diverse tasks per time bucket and cannot currently be fit.
quote: 20% and 80% time horizons are not fully independent estimates from the 50% time horizon, because there aren’t enough parameters to fit them separately. We fit a two-parameter logistic model which doesn’t fit the top and bottom of the success curve separately, so improving performance on 20% horizon tasks can lower 80% horizon .
source: Clarifying limitations of time horizon

claim: Kwa (METR), relaying OpenAI's SWE-Lancer finding: task monetary value (a proxy for engineer-hours) does not correlate with model success rate, so time-length does not predict success on every task distribution; also horizons for visual computer use are 40-100x lower than for software/math.
quote: On SWE-Lancer OpenAI observed that a task’s monetary value (which should be a decent proxy for engineer-hours) doesn’t correlate with a model’s success rate. I still don’t know why this is.
source: Clarifying limitations of time horizon

claim: Across 9 benchmarks (July 2025), software/reasoning domains had 50-200+ minute p50 horizons doubling every 2-6 months, while visual computer use (OSWorld, WebArena) horizons were 40-100x shorter; horizon therefore depends heavily on task domain.
quote: Visual computer use (OSWorld, WebArena) time horizons are 40-100x shorter than the software and reasoning cluster but are increasing at similar rates.
source: How Does Time Horizon Vary Across Domains?

claim: METR's GPT-5.6 Sol predeployment evaluation (TH1.1): p50 ~11.3 h (95% CI 5-40 h) with cheating marked as failure, >270 h if cheating counted as success, 71 h (CI 13-11400 h) if cheating runs are discarded; because of the model's high detected cheating rate METR considers none of these a robust measurement of this model.
original_claim: METR's GPT-5.6 Sol predeployment evaluation (TH1.1): p50 ~11.3 h (95% CI 5-40 h) with cheating marked as failure, >270 h if cheating counted, 71 h (CI 13-11400 h) if cheating runs discarded; METR considers none of these a robust measurement, i.e. by mid-2026 the horizon suite no longer gives a stable frontier number.
quote: With the data we collected for GPT-5.6 Sol, if we follow our standard methodology of marking cheating attempts as failures, we arrive at a 50%-Time Horizon point estimate of around 11.3hrs (95% CI: 5hrs - 40hrs), but if we count the cheating attempts as legitimate successes, the point estimate jumps beyond 270hrs – well beyond the range where we consider our task suite to give reliable measurements.
source: Summary of METR's predeployment evaluation of GPT-5.6 Sol

claim: METR's Claude Opus 5.5 evaluation (2026-09-22) reports no time horizon at all (five AI R&D tasks instead) and judges it an incremental improvement over Fable 5.1 that still shows qualitative weaknesses an expert would not show on hard, long-horizon tasks.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 still has qualitative weaknesses that an expert human is unlikely to exhibit when solving hard, long-horizon tasks or doing open-ended reasoning.
source: Summary of METR's predeployment evaluation of Claude Opus 5.5

claim: On 18 real issues (avg 1.3 maintainer-hours) from stdlib-js and hypothesis, Claude 3.7 Sonnet passed maintainer tests 38% of the time but none of 15 reviewed PRs was mergeable as-is; estimated fix-up time averaged 42 min overall and 26 min even for test-passing PRs, about a third of the task's human time.
quote: Claude 3.7 Sonnet in the Inspect ReAct agent scaffold has an average success rate of 38% (±19%, 95% CI) on these issues, as measured by the maintainer-written test cases, indicating that this agent often implements the core functional components of the issues correctly 5 . However, when manually reviewing a subset of these PRs 6 , none of them are mergeable as-is.
source: Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation

claim: 4 maintainers reviewing 296 AI-generated SWE-bench Verified PRs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet through Claude 4.5 Sonnet and GPT-5; golden patches avg ~17 changed lines) would not merge roughly half of test-passing PRs; maintainer merge rates were ~24 pp below grader scores after normalizing to a 68% golden-patch baseline. METR notes agents had no chance to iterate on feedback.
quote: We find that roughly half of test-passing SWE-bench Verified PRs written by mid-2024 to mid/late-2025 agents would not be merged into main by repo maintainers, even after adjusting for noise in maintainer merge decisions.
source: Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main
by: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)

claim: METR RCT (Feb-Jun 2025, experienced OSS developers on their own repos, tasks averaging two hours, mainly Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet): AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer, against the developers' expected 24% speedup.
quote: Core Result When developers are allowed to use AI tools, they take 19% longer to complete issues—a significant slowdown that goes against developer beliefs and expert forecasts.
source: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
by: METR (Joel Becker, Nate Rush et al.)

claim: METR's follow-up (started Aug 2025, reported 2026-02-24): returning developers' estimated speedup was -18% (CI -38% to +9%) and new developers' -4% (CI -15% to +9%); METR believes developers are likely more sped up now but calls its data an unreliable, likely lower-bound signal because developers declined AI-disallowed work and tasks, pay was cut, and time-spent measurements are unreliable for developers running multiple agents concurrently.
original_claim: METR's follow-up (Aug 2025 start, reported 2026-02-24): returning developers' task-time change was -18% (CI -38% to +9%) and new developers' -4% (CI -15% to +9%), i.e. a probable but unproven speedup; METR calls the data unreliable because developers declined AI-disallowed work and time-on-task is unmeasurable for developers running multiple agents concurrently.
quote: Our early 2025 study found the use of AI causes tasks to take 19% longer, with a confidence interval between +2% and +39%. For the subset of the original developers who participated in the later study, we now estimate a speedup of -18% with a confidence interval between -38% and +9%. Among newly-recruited developers the estimated speedup is -4%, with a confidence interval between -15% and +9%.
source: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
by: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (METR)

claim: Sinha et al. (ICLR 2026): with knowledge and plan supplied, per-step accuracy still degrades as step count rises, partly via 'self-conditioning' (errors already in context make further errors likelier), which model scale does not fix but thinking mitigates; marginal single-step gains compound into exponential gains in completable task length.
quote: We then observe that the per-step accuracy of models degrades as the number of steps increases. This is not just due to long-context limitations -- curiously, we observe a self-conditioning effect -- models become more likely to make mistakes when the context contains their errors from prior turns. Self-conditioning does not reduce by just scaling the model size.
source: The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs
by: Akshit Sinha, Arvindh Arun, Shashwat Goel, Steffen Staab, Jonas Geiping

claim: Single-turn execution length (synthetic key-sum task, 2025 models): GPT-5 thinking executed 2176 steps vs Claude-4 Sonnet 432, Grok 4 384, Gemini 2.5 Pro 120; without thinking, even the largest models fail beyond a few steps. Re-verifies research-2026-09-22's 2509.09677 entry: supported.
quote: We find a surprisingly large gap between GPT-5 (codenamed Horizon ) with 2176 steps and others like Claude-4 Sonnet (432 steps), Grok 4 (384 steps), and Gemini 2.5 Pro (120 steps).
source: The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs

claim: Toby Ord (May 2025) showed METR's suite results could be fit by a constant hazard rate per human-minute (exponential decline, p50 as a half-life), implying T80 ~ 1/3, T90 ~ 1/7, T99 ~ 1/70, T99.9 ~ 1/700 of T50 on that suite; his 4 Feb 2026 update on the page says newer analysis shows agents probably do not follow a constant hazard rate, since their hazard declines as a task goes on.
original_claim: Toby Ord models METR's data as a constant hazard rate per human-minute, so success falls exponentially with task length and the p50 horizon is a half-life; this predicts T80 ~ 1/3 T50, T90 ~ 1/7, T99 ~ 1/70, T99.9 ~ 1/700 (each extra nine divides by 10), and doubling task length squares the success probability.
quote: I show that within their suite of research-engineering tasks the performance of AI agents on longer-duration tasks can be explained by an extremely simple mathematical model — a constant rate of failing during each minute a human would take to do the task. This implies an exponentially declining success rate with the length of the task and that each agent could be characterised by its own half-life.
source: Is there a Half-Life for the Success Rates of AI Agents?

claim: Ord's 2025 rule of thumb, derived from a constant-hazard model of METR's suite and not separately measured, puts T90 at about 1/7 and T99 at about 1/70 of T50; Ord's Feb 2026 update says agents probably do not follow a constant hazard rate, which undercuts these ratios.
original_claim: Ord's rule of thumb (derived from the constant-hazard model, not separately measured): high-reliability horizons are far shorter than p50 — about 1/7 of it at 90% and 1/70 at 99%.
quote: T $_{80}$ ≈ 1/3 T $_{50}$ T $_{90}$ ≈ 1/7 T $_{50}$ T $_{99}$ ≈ 1/70 T $_{50}$ T $_{99.9}$ ≈ 1/700 T $_{50}$ [and each additional ‘nine’ of reliability beyond this divides the time horizon by 10]
source: Is there a Half-Life for the Success Rates of AI Agents?

claim: Chroma's Context Rot report (18 LLMs incl. GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3) holds task complexity fixed and finds performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows; on LongMemEval, models that succeed on focused (relevant-only) input degrade consistently on the full ~113k-token input.
quote: Our results reveal that models do not use their context uniformly; instead, their performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows.
source: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance
by: Kelly Hong, Anton Troynikov, Jeff Huber (Chroma)

claim: SWE-bench-Live (OpenHands + Claude 3.7 Sonnet): single-file gold patches under 5 lines were solved 48% of the time; at 3+ files or >100 lines success fell below 10%; patches touching 7+ files were never solved.
quote: Success is high when the fix is local: a single-file patch that changes fewer than five lines is solved almost one time in two (48%). Performance degrades quickly as either dimension grows. Once the patch edits three or more files, or spans more than one hundred lines, the success rate falls below ten per-cent; patches that touch seven or more files are never solved.
source: SWE-bench Goes Live!

claim: SWE-Bench Pro (Scale AI; gold patches avg 107.4 lines across 4.1 files; all models <45% Pass@1): resolve rate is relatively stable for single-file problems and declines sharply as file count grows; beyond 3 files the frontier/open gap widens, with Claude Opus 4.1 and GPT-5 still above 10% even at 10+ files while open models approach zero (analysis run with a 50-turn/$2 cap).
original_claim: SWE-Bench Pro (Scale AI; gold patches avg 107.4 lines across 4.1 files; best models <45% Pass@1 in late 2025): resolve rate is stable for single-file problems and falls sharply as file count grows; Claude Opus 4.1 and GPT-5 stay above 10% only at 10+ files while open models approach zero.
quote: Models maintain relatively stable performance for single-file problems but exhibit sharp declines as file count increases. Notably, the performance gap between frontier and smaller models widens dramatically beyond 3 files, with Claude Opus 4.1 and OpenAI GPT-5 maintaining above 10% resolve rates even for problems involving 10+ files, while open-source alternatives approach near-zero performance.
source: SWE-Bench Pro: Can AI Agents Solve Long-Horizon Software Engineering Tasks?

claim: Re-verifies research-2026-09-22 ('success falls with spread'): SWE-EVO v6 (48 tasks; gold patches avg 20.9 files / 610.5 lines) shows the SAME model gpt-5.2 at 72.80% on SWE-bench Verified vs 22.92% on SWE-EVO (best model gpt-5.4 25%); on SWE-Bench ProMax (2608.09802, 11.4 files / 261.6 lines) gpt-5.2 is the best model at 41.2%; instances no model-scaffold resolves average 14.84 linked PRs vs 1.67 for the easiest group. The earlier record's numbers hold; its gloss 'at one or two files' for SWE-bench Verified is not stated in these sources.
quote: Even the strongest model gpt-5.4 resolves only around 25% of SWE-EVO instances, and matched-model comparisons show the same pattern: gpt-5.2 drops from 72.80% on SWE-bench Verified to 22.92% on SWE-EVO .
source: SWE-EVO: Benchmarking Coding Agents in Long-Horizon Software Evolution Scenarios

claim: SWE-Bench ProMax (COLM 2026; 170 refactoring tasks avg 11.4 files / 261.6 lines; best GPT-5.2 41.2%): Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Kimi-K2.5 track the gold file-count distribution for patches up to ~5 files, but their per-instance file-count CDF reaches 90% by ~10 files where the gold patch CDF needs ~20; the authors name incomplete cross-file propagation as the dominant failure, and failed runs consume more interaction rounds. (Route: quote confirmed on 2026-09-26 in the arXiv HTML page, which renders the tilde as MathML.)
original_claim: SWE-Bench ProMax (COLM 2026; 170 refactoring tasks avg 11.4 files / 261.6 lines; best GPT-5.2 41.2%): the dominant failure is incomplete propagation — Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Kimi-K2.5 track the gold file count up to ~5 files, but reach 90% of their edits by ~10 files where gold needs ~20; failed runs also use more interaction rounds.
quote: Both Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Kimi-K2.5 closely track the gold patch distribution for small changes (up to ∼5 files), but diverge sharply for larger patches: whereas the gold patch CDF reaches 90% only around 20 files, both agents reach 90% by approximately 10 files. This indicates that the dominant failure mode is incomplete refactoring —agents identify and modify some affected files but fail to propagate changes to all locations requiring coordinated updates.
source: SWE-Bench ProMax: Benchmarking Agents on Large-Scale Multilingual Code Refactoring

claim: Over 14,922 trajectories of two model families at three scales on five benchmarks, resolved runs concentrate in the low Spread-Novelty-Centrality region for every family and scale, while the behavioural signature of success is family-specific: Claude succeeds by matching gold scope (file parity share 0.17 at smallest to 0.54 at largest scale), Qwen by exceeding gold scope at every scale, and editing too little marks failure for both; the authors caution that the families ran under different harnesses (Claude Code vs Qwen Code), so the contrast may reflect the harness as much as the model.
original_claim: stronger models succeed by matching the gold patch's file count (parity 0.17 → 0.54 with scale), weaker ones by exceeding it
quote: Claude succeeds by matching the scope of the gold solution, and its parity share on files rises from $0.17$ at the smallest scale to $0.54$ at the largest. Qwen succeeds by exceeding the gold scope at every scale, and editing too little marks failure for both families.
source: What Does an Agentic Software Engineering Benchmark Measure? Profiling Task Demands and Agent Behaviour Beyond What Category Labels Reveal

claim: SlopCodeBench (36 problems, 196 checkpoints, 15 agents): when agents repeatedly extend their own code, core pass rate falls from 64.6% to 35.5% across checkpoints, cost per checkpoint grows 2.2x, no agent solves any problem end-to-end (best strict rate 14.8%, GPT 5.5), and structural erosion rises in 77% of trajectories. Re-verifies research-2026-09-22's 2603.24755 entry: supported (the 64.6->35.5 figure is the core pass rate).
quote: Core pass rate falls from 64.6% to 35.5%.
source: SlopCodeBench: Benchmarking How Coding Agents Degrade Over Long-Horizon Iterative Tasks

claim: MAKER (Towers of Hanoi, >1M LLM steps, zero errors): with maximal decomposition (one step per microagent) plus first-to-ahead-by-k voting, cost scales log-linearly in step count s, Theta(p^-m c s ln s); cost grows exponentially in m, the number of decisions assigned to one agent. Re-verifies research-2026-09-22's 2511.09030 entry: supported (Theta(cs ln s) is the m=1 case); the task is synthetic, not coding.
quote: Notably, the cost grows exponentially with m . Figure 5 illustrates this phenomenon. As the number of meaningful decisions assigned to an agent grows, the chance that its sequence of decisions will match exactly across multiple samples vanishes.
source: Solving a Million-Step LLM Task with Zero Errors
by: Elliot Meyerson et al. (Cognizant AI Lab)

claim: Single controlled study (fixed 24-turn planning agent, three models): at 5x context compression no model's completion changed significantly while retrieval calls rose (GPT-5.5 completion 80%->85%, n.s.; retrieval 21.0->63.9 calls); in ALFWorld there was no retrieval surge, so the authors conclude compression can impose hidden reacquisition costs that completion metrics may not expose, depending on the environment.
original_claim: Controlled compression study (fixed 24-turn planning agent, three models): at 5x context compression completion rates did not change significantly, but agents re-fetched dropped state — GPT-5.5 completion 80%->85% (n.s.) while retrieval calls rose 21.0->63.9; task-completion metrics hide the cost of compaction.
quote: GPT-5.5 is the clearest case: completion changes from 80% to 85% (p = 1.0) while retrieval increases from 21.0 to 63.9 calls (p = .002).
source: What Does Context Compression Cost an Agent? Interaction Costs Unrevealed by Task-Completion Metrics

claim: Preliminary empirical study (AppWorld): recurrent context compression in long-horizon agents can weaken the influence of recent interactions, increasing blocked actions, repeated exploration and run-to-run instability.
quote: In this preliminary empirical study, we show that compression can weaken the influence of recent interactions, increasing blocked actions, repeated exploration, and instability across runs.
source: Toward Reliable Context Compression for Long-Horizon Agents: An Empirical Study of Execution Instability

claim: Anthropic (Opus 4.5 on the Claude Agent SDK, Nov 2025): handed one high-level prompt ('build a clone of claude.ai') and looping across context windows with compaction, the agent tried to do the whole thing at once, ran out of context mid-feature and left the next session a half-built, undocumented state. Too-large-at-once is named as the first failure mode of long runs.
quote: First, the agent tended to try to do too much at once—essentially to attempt to one-shot the app. Often, this led to the model running out of context in the middle of its implementation, leaving the next session to start with a feature half-implemented and undocumented.
source: Effective harnesses for long-running agents

claim: Anthropic's fix had an initializer agent expand the user's single high-level prompt into a comprehensive JSON feature list (over 200 end-to-end features for the claude.ai clone, all initially 'failing') that later coding sessions consume; the list was agent-written.
original_claim: Anthropic's fix kept the whole outcome as ONE handed-over task and moved decomposition inside it: an initializer agent expanded the user's single prompt into a JSON feature list (over 200 end-to-end features for the claude.ai clone, all initially 'failing'), which later sessions consume. The human did not author or accept the 200 items.
quote: we prompted the initializer agent to write a comprehensive file of feature requirements expanding on the user’s initial prompt. In the claude.ai clone example, this meant over 200 features
source: Effective harnesses for long-running agents

claim: Within that agent-owned feature list, each coding session worked on exactly one feature, committed to git and updated a progress file; Anthropic calls one-feature-at-a-time 'critical' for Opus 4.5-era models (its 2026-03 follow-up later dropped this decomposition for Opus 4.6, see sizing-lab-7).
quote: the next iteration of the coding agent was then asked to work on only one feature at a time. This incremental approach turned out to be critical to addressing the agent’s tendency to do too much at once.
source: Effective harnesses for long-running agents

claim: Anthropic Labs (Opus 4.5, retro game maker prompt, one run each): a solo agent ran 20 min for $9 and shipped a broken core feature; a planner/generator/evaluator harness ran 6 h for $200 (>20x cost) and produced a working app. Bigger, longer, structured runs bought quality at a large token premium.
quote: The harness was over 20x more expensive, but the difference in output quality was immediately apparent.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: In the same harness the decomposition was agent-owned: a planner turned a 1-sentence prompt into a 16-feature spec over ten sprints, and generator/evaluator agents negotiated granular per-sprint contracts (Sprint 3 alone had 27 criteria) with no human in that loop.
quote: the planner step expanded that prompt into a 16-feature spec spread across ten sprints.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: Without a planning step the generator under-scoped: given only the raw prompt it built a less feature-rich app. Anthropic kept the planner even after simplifying the harness; the force here is toward a fuller spec inside the task, not smaller tasks.
quote: Without the planner, the generator under-scoped: given the raw prompt, it would start building without first speccing its work, and end up creating a less feature-rich application than the planner did.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: With Opus 4.6 Anthropic removed the sprint decomposition entirely (context resets had already been dropped for Opus 4.5); the builder ran coherently for over two hours without sprints (whole V2 run: 3 h 50 min, $124.70, one DAW build). The post frames harness components such as sprints as assumptions about model limits that go stale as models improve.
original_claim: With Opus 4.6 Anthropic removed the sprint decomposition (and context resets) entirely; the builder ran coherently for over two hours in one pass (whole V2 run: 3 h 50 min, $124.70, one DAW build). claim: A separate evaluator/QA pass is worth its cost only when the task sits beyond what the current model does reliably solo; inside that boundary it is overhead. Review depth should track task difficulty relative to the model.
quote: The practical implication is that the evaluator is not a fixed yes-or-no decision. It is worth the cost when the task sits beyond what the current model does reliably solo.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: General principle from the same post: each harness component (including task decomposition) encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do, and these assumptions go stale as models improve, so should be re-tested at each model release.
quote: every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own, and those assumptions are worth stress testing, both because they may be incorrect, and because they can quickly go stale as models improve.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: Anthropic names sub-agents as one of three long-horizon techniques (with compaction and note-taking): a subagent may spend tens of thousands of tokens exploring but hands back a 1,000-2,000-token summary, keeping the lead agent's context clean.

source: Effective context engineering for AI agents

claim: Anthropic's production data (Claude 4 era, research product): agents use ~4x the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems ~15x; multi-agent is only economical where task value pays for it.
quote: In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats.
source: How we built our multi-agent research system

claim: Anthropic (June 2025) judged coding a poor fit for multi-agent decomposition: fewer truly parallelizable subtasks than research, and agents then weak at real-time coordination and delegation. Later Anthropic model guides (Opus 5, Fable 5) claim much better subagent coordination, so this is dated for current models.

claim: When a lead agent decomposes work, each delegated piece needs an objective, output format, tool guidance and explicit boundaries; vague one-line delegations ('research the semiconductor shortage') produced duplicated work and gaps.
quote: Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information.
source: How we built our multi-agent research system

claim: Claude Code best practices (undated docs, read 2026-09-26): a planning step is overhead for small, clear changes; its floor test is whether the diff can be described in one sentence. Planning pays when the approach is uncertain or the change spans multiple files.
quote: If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.
source: Best practices for Claude Code

claim: Claude Code docs: without a runnable check the human becomes the verification loop for every mistake; a pass/fail check (optionally enforced via /goal or a Stop hook) is what lets an unattended run finish without the person. Verification, not task smallness, is the named lever for walking away.
quote: Without a check it can run, “looks done” is the only signal available, and you become the verification loop: every mistake waits for you to notice it.
source: Best practices for Claude Code

claim: Claude Code docs: reset context between unrelated tasks; after two failed corrections on the same issue start fresh with a better prompt. The unit boundary is 'unrelated task', not a size.
quote: A clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms a long session with accumulated corrections.
source: Best practices for Claude Code

claim: Claude Code docs put the human's time into the up-front spec rather than supervision: self-contained specs name files and interfaces, state out-of-scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step.
quote: Time spent making the spec precise pays off more than time spent watching the implementation.
source: Best practices for Claude Code

claim: Claude Code docs: for large migrations the agent itself splits the change — /batch fans one instruction out to 5-30 subagents, each in its own worktree — so decomposition of a large change is delegated to the tool, not pre-cut by the human.
quote: Run /batch <instruction> to have Claude split the change across 5 to 30 subagents.
source: Best practices for Claude Code

claim: Claude Code docs: the longer an unattended run, the more an independent fresh-context review of the diff matters before counting the work done — longer autonomous tasks shift, not remove, review cost.
quote: The longer Claude works unattended, the more an independent check matters before you count the work as done.
source: Best practices for Claude Code

claim: Claude Code agent-teams docs give a two-sided task-size rule for work handed to a teammate: too small and coordination overhead exceeds benefit; too large and teammates run too long without check-ins, risking wasted effort; just right is a self-contained unit with a clear deliverable (a function, a test file, a review). (Route: quote confirmed on 2026-09-26 at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams.md, the Markdown route of the docs page.)

claim: Claude Code docs: agent teams add coordination overhead and significantly more tokens; for sequential tasks, same-file edits or heavily dependent work, one session (or subagents) is more effective.
quote: Agent teams add coordination overhead and use significantly more tokens than a single session. They work best when teammates can operate independently. For sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents are more effective.

claim: Claude Code /goal docs target 'substantial work with a verifiable end state' judged by a separate evaluator after every turn; its listed examples include implementing a design doc until all acceptance criteria hold and working through a labeled issue backlog until the queue is empty, each as one goal. claim: Anthropic's Opus 5 guide: the model over-delegates; delegation pays only on genuinely independent, sizeable tracks and multiplies cost and time on small tasks. Suggested rule: do not delegate work finishable in a handful of tool calls.
quote: Delegation pays off on genuinely independent, sizeable tracks of work, but it multiplies cost and time when applied to small tasks.

claim: Anthropic says Opus 5 coordinates subagent teams well (writer-verifier patterns, few overwrites) — a claimed reversal of the June 2025 view that agents coordinate poorly.

claim: Anthropic's Fable 5 guide pushes toward LARGER handed-over tasks: the model is most effective on end-to-end work that takes a person hours, days or weeks; testing only on simpler workloads undersells it. It recommends letting the model scope the task itself.

claim: Fable 5 guide: hand a harder task and let the model do its own scoping and clarification before executing — scoping is moved from the human to the agent.

source: Prompting Claude Fable 5

claim: Fable 5 guide on human checkpoints in long runs: pause for the person only for destructive/irreversible actions, real scope changes, or input only they can give — not per step or per sub-task.
quote: Pause for the user only when the work genuinely requires them: a destructive or irreversible action, a real scope change, or input that only they can provide.
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5

claim: Fable 5 guide: for long runs, schedule periodic verification by separate fresh-context verifier subagents against the spec, which tend to outperform self-critique — review is built into the long task rather than done by splitting it.
quote: Separate, fresh-context verifier subagents tend to outperform self-critique.
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5

claim: Anthropic's Opus 5.5 guide claims it sustains multi-hour audits and migrations of large codebases end to end, with parallel subagents and little oversight.

original_claim: Parallel agents helped only while work split into many independent units (distinct failing tests); on one indivisible task (compiling the kernel) all 16 agents hit the same bug and overwrote each other, until a GCC-oracle harness re-split it. claim: OpenAI's agent-building guide (Apr 2025): maximize one agent first; split into multiple agents only when instructions/tool choice fail, because more agents add complexity and overhead.

claim: Cognition (Walden Yan, June 2025) argues against splitting a task into parallel subagent subtasks: each subagent's actions embed implicit decisions that conflict with siblings' (Flappy Bird example), so the default should be a single-threaded linear agent with continuous context; for very long tasks, add history compression rather than parallel writers.
quote: Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results … The simplest way to follow the principles is to just use a single-threaded linear agent
source: Don't Build Multi-Agents

claim: Ten months later (April 2026) Cognition reports its original objection still holds for parallel-writer swarms; the multi-agent patterns that work in production keep writes single-threaded (one writer, others contribute review/advice).
quote: Our original observations still hold today for parallel-writer swarms: most of the sexy ideas in that space still don’t see meaningful adoption. But we've found a narrower class of patterns that do: setups where multiple agents contribute intelligence to a task while writes stay single-threaded.
source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working

claim: Cognition observes that as agent usage exploded (~8x in its largest enterprise segment over 6 months), users became bottlenecked on the human work around agents — management, planning and reviewing — which is what pushed them toward agents managing agents and agent-vs-review-agent loops.

source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working

claim: Cognition ships a 'manager Devin' that takes larger scope (a feature spanning ten PRs, a week of work), splits it and coordinates child Devins; it reports coherence required substantial extra context engineering: managers default to over-prescriptive delegation, assume shared state with children, and don't relay cross-agent discoveries by default. source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working

source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working
