source: When to use Devin (Devin docs)

claim: On Latent Space (May 2026), Cole Murray (OpenInspect) dates a shift to ~December 2025 (Opus 4.5, GPT-5.2): background agents could go from a good-enough spec to a completed PR with little friction, which made background agents practical.
quote: we could pretty much go from a specification to a completed pull request, assuming the spec was good enough, with very little friction. And that paradigm alone, I think, changed a lot of how we interact with agents, and opened this world where background agents became more practical.
source: The Age of Async Agents — Cognition's Walden Yan & OpenInspect's Cole Murray (Latent Space)
by: Cole Murray, Walden Yan, swyx (Latent Space)

claim: Same episode: despite giving Devins an MCP to message and spawn other Devins, day-to-day practice is still mostly one Devin; the surprising success was a single long-running Devin doing its own context management on a very large task (rebuilding a Windows OS system) rather than a swarm. (Transcript attributes these lines to Cole Murray; content describes Cognition's own experience.)
quote: we’ve still found that most practical use on a day-to-day basis has been one single Devin. … We found a surprising success of, don’t do a swarm or anything, just have one Devin, it does its own context management. Just let it keep running for a while and give it some crazy tasks.
source: The Age of Async Agents — Cognition's Walden Yan & OpenInspect's Cole Murray (Latent Space)
by: Cole Murray, Walden Yan, swyx (Latent Space)

claim: Willison (Oct 2025, Claude Code Sonnet 4.5 / Codex GPT-5-Codex) names review as the natural bottleneck on agent output: he can review and land only one significant change at a time, so parallel agents are reserved for research, small maintenance, and carefully specified work; code built from his own detailed spec is much cheaper to review than code 'out of nowhere'.
quote: AI-generated code needs to be reviewed, which means the natural bottleneck on all of this is how fast I can review the results. … I can only focus on reviewing and landing one significant change at a time
source: Embracing the parallel coding agent lifestyle

claim: Willison's Agentic Engineering Patterns guide (anti-patterns chapter, ~March 2026) says a good agent-produced PR is small enough for efficient review, and several small PRs beat one big one — splitting into commits is cheap because the agent can do the git work. This is about the reviewer's load, not the agent's capability.
quote: The change is small enough to be reviewed efficiently without inflicting too much additional cognitive load on the reviewer. Several small PRs beats one big one, and splitting code into separate commits is easy with a coding agent to do the Git finagling for you.
source: Anti-patterns: things to avoid — Agentic Engineering Patterns

claim: Karpathy (YC AI Startup School keynote, June 2025) describes his own AI-assisted coding as small incremental chunks on a single concrete thing, fearing large diffs, to keep the human generate-verify loop fast; he frames autonomy as a slider tuned to task complexity ('keep the AI on the leash').
quote: in my own work, I’m always scared to get way too big diffs. I always go in small incremental chunks. I want to make sure that everything is good. I want to spin this loop very, very fast. And I sort of work on small chunks of single concrete thing.
source: Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again) — transcript
by: Andrej Karpathy (transcript by The Singju Post)

claim: By January 2026 Karpathy reports moving from ~20% to ~80% agent coding (Nov→Dec 2025) and operating in large 'code actions'; he recommends declarative success criteria (tests first, loops) so agents loop longer (this sweep reads that as a move away from his June 2025 small-chunk framing; he does not say so himself), while still calling agent-swarm hype premature and advising watching agents 'like a hawk' on code you care about.
quote: Change your approach from imperative to declarative to get the agents looping longer and gain leverage. … Both the "no need for IDE anymore" hype and the "agent swarm" hype is imo too much for right now.
source: A few random notes from claude coding quite a bit last few weeks (X post; verbatim text via api.fxtwitter.com)

claim: Harper Reed's spec->plan->execute workflow (Feb 2025) has a reasoning model break a blueprint into small iterative chunks, then into small steps again, iterating until steps are 'right sized': small enough to implement safely (with strong testing in the TDD variant) but big enough to move the project forward, each prompt building on the previous with no orphaned code.
original_claim: Harper Reed's widely copied spec→plan→execute workflow (Feb 2025) has the LLM decompose a blueprint twice into 'right sized' steps: small enough to implement safely with strong testing, big enough to move forward, each prompt building on the previous with no orphaned code.
quote: break it down into small, iterative chunks that build on each other. Look at these chunks and then go another round to break it into small steps. Review the results and make sure that the steps are small enough to be implemented safely with strong testing, but big enough to move the project forward.
source: My LLM codegen workflow atm

claim: Addy Osmani (Jan 2026) recommends breaking work into iterative steps or tickets tackled one at a time (one function / bug / feature per prompt), citing reports that large one-shot generations produce inconsistency and duplication 'like 10 devs worked on it without talking to each other'; each chunk becomes its own commit or PR.
quote: we break the project into iterative steps or tickets and tackle them one by one . This mirrors good software engineering practice, but it’s even more important with AI in the loop. LLMs do best when given focused prompts: implement one function, fix one bug, add one feature at a time.
source: My LLM coding workflow going into 2026

claim: Mitchell Hashimoto (Feb 2026) learned to split agent work into separate clear, actionable task sessions rather than one 'draw the owl' mega-session, and to separate planning from execution sessions for vague requests; in his end-of-day pattern agents mostly finished in under half an hour.
quote: Break down sessions into separate clear, actionable tasks. Don't try to "draw the owl" in one mega session. For vague requests, split the work into separate planning vs. execution sessions.
source: My AI Adoption Journey

claim: Hashimoto (Feb 2026) runs one background agent at a time and is not running multiple agents; he estimates he is effective at having one running 10-20% of a working day, and says part of the challenge is improving his own workflows and tools to have a constant stream of high-quality delegable work.
original_claim: Hashimoto runs one background agent at a time (not parallel) and reports it active only 10–20% of his working day; the limiting factor he names is his own supply of high-quality delegable work, not agent capacity.
quote: I'd say right now I'm maybe effective at having a background agent running 10 to 20% of a normal working day. … Part of the challenge of this goal is improving my own workflows and tools so that I can have a constant stream of high quality work to do that I can delegate.
source: My AI Adoption Journey

claim: Kent Beck (April 2026), after using a coordinator/implementer/verifier multi-agent tool, reports he ended up managing the swarm himself — tracking which agent did what and holding state in his head — and argues what he wants is outcome-orientation (describe the result, have the tool say if it's achievable), not agents or swarms.
quote: I was managing it. Watching which agent was doing what. Wondering when to interrupt. Holding state in my head that the system should have been holding for me. … Multi-agent is a feature. Outcome-orientation is the thing the feature is supposed to deliver.
source: Genie Lessons: Nobody Wants Agents

claim: Geoffrey Huntley's 'Ralph' loop (July 2025) runs one agent process in a loop doing exactly one item per loop with fresh context, where the agent itself picks the most important item from a maintained fix_plan.md; the item size may be relaxed as the project matures and narrowed again if it goes off the rails. Small execution units, but the human does not hand-size each one.
quote: One item per loop. I need to repeat myself here—one item per loop. You may relax this restriction as the project progresses, but if it starts going off the rails, then you need to narrow it down to just one item.
source: Ralph Wiggum as a "software engineer"

claim: In Ralph, the human's control point is the agent-maintained TODO list (fix_plan.md), not individual tickets: Huntley watches it closely and repeatedly throws it away and regenerates it.
quote: The TODO list is what I'm watching like a hawk. And I throw it out often.
source: Ralph Wiggum as a "software engineer"

claim: Steve Yegge's Gas Town (Jan 2026; read via Wayback copy since Medium blocks curl) casts the human as product manager whose job is to make tasks for agents, asserting Opus 4.5 handles 'any reasonably sized task'; 'molecules' chain small sequenced beads so hours of work (or a whole weekend of swarming) can be set up in advance and survive crashes and compaction. (Route: quote confirmed on 2026-09-26 through a web.archive.org copy, since the page returns 403 to a plain fetch.)
quote: Opus 4.5 can handle any reasonably sized task, so your job is to make tasks for it. That’s it. … I wanted to do it in advance, so I could set up hours of work ahead of time, which they would execute atomically in the right order.
source: Welcome to Gas Town

claim: Yegge reports that swarming many workers immediately creates a merge-queue problem — the baseline moves so far that late workers must reimagine and reimplement their changes — which he solved with a dedicated merge agent (Refinery) merging one at a time. (Route: quote confirmed on 2026-09-26 through a web.archive.org copy, since the page returns 403 to a plain fetch.)
quote: As soon as you start swarming workers, you run into the Merge Queue (MQ) problem. Your workers get into a monkey knife fight over rebasing/merging and it can get ugly. The baseline can change so much during a swarm that the final workers getting merged are trying to merge against an unrecognizable new head.
source: Welcome to Gas Town

claim: Yegge ('The AI Vampire', Feb 2026, quoted by Simon Willison) reports that agentic engineering leaves the human only the hard decisions and summaries, and that he can sustain that pace only in bursts of a few hours once or twice a day — Willison summarizes this as about four hours of agent work a day being realistic.
quote: I’ve argued that AI has turned us all into Jeff Bezos, by automating the easy work, and leaving us with all the difficult decisions, summaries, and problem-solving. I find that I am only really comfortable working at that pace for short bursts of a few hours once or occasionally twice a day, even with lots of practice.
source: The AI Vampire (link post quoting Steve Yegge)
by: Steve Yegge, quoted by Simon Willison

claim: Stripe's 'minions' (Feb 2026) are fully unattended agents built to one-shot tasks from a Slack message to a CI-passing PR with no interaction in between; >1,000 merged PRs/week are fully minion-written (human-reviewed). Stripe names developer attention as a most-constrained resource and describes engineers spinning up many minions in parallel for many small issues (e.g., during on-call).
quote: in a world where one of our most constrained resources is developer attention, unattended agents allow for parallelization of tasks. … We frequently see engineers spinning up multiple minions in parallel, to enable them to parallelize the completion of many different tasks. This can be particularly helpful during an on-call rotation to effectively resolve many small issues that might arise.
source: Minions: Stripe's one-shot, end-to-end coding agents

claim: Spotify's background coding agent team (Honk, Nov 2025) advises one change per prompt: combining several related changes into one elaborate prompt tends to exhaust the context window or yield a partial result. (Their earlier homegrown loop worked well only for small changes such as a manifest edit, a config flag, or a single line.)
quote: Do one change at a time. It can be convenient for users to combine several related changes into one elaborate prompt, but it’s more likely to get the agent in trouble because it will exhaust its context window or it will deliver a partial result.
source: Background Coding Agents: Context Engineering (Honk, Part 2)

claim: Spotify reports (internal metrics, thousands of agent sessions) an LLM judge comparing diff to prompt vetoes about a quarter of sessions, most commonly for the agent going outside the prompt's scope; after a veto the agent course-corrects about half the time. They call reviewing nonsensical PRs expensive for engineers.
quote: out of thousands of agent sessions, the judge vetoes about a quarter of them. When that happens, the agent is able to course correct half the time. From empirical observations, we have seen that the most common trigger is the agent going outside the instructions outlined in the prompt.
source: Background Coding Agents: Predictable Results Through Strong Feedback Loops (Honk, Part 3)

claim: Ramp (Jan 2026) reports its in-house background agent Inspect writes ~30% of PRs merged to its frontend and backend repos after a couple of months; because sessions are fast and effectively free, builders run unlimited concurrent sessions and even launch multiple versions of the same prompt to see which lands. (Article text read from the site's JS bundle; the page is client-rendered.) (Route: quote confirmed on 2026-09-26 in the site's JavaScript bundle (the page is JavaScript-only).)
quote: A builder can kick off multiple versions of the same prompt, and just see which one lands. … ~30% of all pull requests merged to our frontend and backend repos are written by Inspect.
source: Why We Built Our Own Background Agent
by: Zach Bruggeman, Jason Quense, Rahul Sengottuvelu (Ramp)

claim: Ryan Lopopolo (OpenAI Frontier, Latent Space, Apr 2026) reports his team went from ~3.5 to 5–10 PRs per engineer per day after GPT-5.2, and humans were exhausted by context-switching across agent sessions; so they built Symphony to take humans out of the loop, making human review a cheap binary merge-or-rework where rework discards the worktree and restarts from scratch.
quote: We were up in the five to 10 PRS per day per engineer. And I don’t know about y’all, but like it’s very taxing to constantly be switching like that. … In Symphony, there’s this like rework state where once the PR is proposed and it’s escalated to the human for review, it should be a cheap review. It is either mergeable or it is not.
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier & Symphony (Latent Space)

claim: Lopopolo names synchronous human attention as the only fundamentally scarce resource, and says multi-human, multi-agent work forced a 45-minute daily standup and an over-decomposed architecture (~500 npm packages for a ~7-person team) so people's agent streams don't trample each other.
quote: The only fundamentally scarce thing is the synchronous human attention of my team. … we have to find ways to carve up the space so people are not trampling on each other.
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier & Symphony (Latent Space)

claim: Cursor (Feb 2026) reports its long-running agent harness produced substantially larger PRs with merge rates comparable to other agents, with preview runs of 25–36 hours; because a slightly wrong assumption compounds over a long autonomous run, the agent proposes a plan and waits for approval before executing.
quote: The results show that long-running agents produced substantially larger PRs with merge rates comparable to other agents. … When the agent goes off and works on a larger task autonomously, a slightly wrong assumption can turn into a completely incorrect solution by the end.
source: Expanding our long-running agents research preview

claim: Cursor's research on hundreds of concurrent agents running for weeks (Jan 2026) found flat self-coordination failed (locks bottlenecked 20 agents to the throughput of 2–3; agents became risk-averse and made small safe changes); a planner/worker/judge hierarchy worked, and 'the right amount of structure is somewhere in the middle'. They also found GPT-5.2 better at extended autonomous work than Opus 4.5, which stopped earlier.
quote: With no hierarchy, agents became risk-averse. They avoided difficult tasks and made small, safe changes instead. No agent took responsibility for hard problems or end-to-end implementation. … The right amount of structure is somewhere in the middle. Too little structure and agents conflict, duplicate work, and drift. Too much structure creates fragility.
source: Scaling long-running autonomous coding

claim: Factory's Missions launch (byline reads 'February 26, 2025' but content and the product launch are Feb 2026) reports vendor telemetry: interactive Droid sessions have a median of ~8 minutes (60% within 15 min), whereas missions have a median of ~2 hours, 37% over four hours, 14% over 24 hours, longest 16 days — outcome-sized work decomposed by an orchestrator into milestones and fresh-context feature workers.
quote: Normal Droid sessions are interactive. Fast back-and-forth: the median session lasts about 8 minutes, with 60% finishing within 15 minutes. … The median mission runs for about 2 hours. 65% run longer than an hour. 37% run longer than four hours.
source: Introducing Missions

claim: Factory lists worker scope as an open trade-off: narrow worker scope keeps agents focused but raises cost and coordination overhead; broad scope keeps continuity but thins attention. They also report serial execution with targeted parallelism beat broad parallelism, and that the orchestrator 'still scopes too broadly sometimes'.
quote: Worker scope. Narrow scope keeps workers focused but increases overall cost and introduces more coordination overhead. Broad scope maintains continuity within features, but stretches each agent's attention thinner.
source: Introducing Missions

claim: Factory's Missions docs (undated; accessed 2026-09-26) give a feature-count heuristic (a few straightforward features: normal session; about 1-500: a Mission; more than 500: split) and call it 'a planning heuristic, not a hard limit'; the more important question is whether the work has a clear outcome and divides into meaningful milestones.
original_claim: Factory's Missions docs (undated; accessed 2026-09-26) size the choice by outcome rather than a count: a few straightforward features go in a normal session; larger multi-feature work goes to a Mission; the deciding question is whether the work has a clear outcome and divides into meaningful milestones.
quote: These numbers are a planning heuristic, not a hard limit. The more important question is whether the work has a clear outcome and can be divided into meaningful milestones.
source: Factory Missions (docs)

claim: Amp's Lewis Metcalf (Dec 2025, Opus 4.5 era) worked in short threads that each do one thing; one shipped feature was ~13 threads averaging ~80k tokens, biggest 151k output tokens, and he equated short threads with small tasks. The note is now marked 'Archived': Amp says it was written for an older model and context-window era and that with auto-compaction going beyond 200k tokens is now fine.
original_claim: Amp's team (Lewis Metcalf, Dec 2025) works in short threads that each do one thing (one change per thread); one shipped feature was a cluster of ~13 threads averaging ~80k tokens, largest 151k output tokens — equating 'short threads' with 'small tasks' while the feature remains the unit the human tracks.
quote: Breaking into short threads == breaking into small tasks. Big tasks are best broken down into small tasks. This was true before the agents came, and it’s true now that they’re here.
source: 200k Tokens Is Plenty

claim: GitHub's Copilot coding agent docs (undated; accessed 2026-09-26) say the assigned issue is effectively the prompt; ideal issues are clear, well-scoped, with complete acceptance criteria and file directions; complex/broadly scoped, cross-repo, ambiguous, or production-critical work is better kept by the developer.
quote: GitHub Copilot provides better results when assigned clear, well-scoped tasks. … it's useful to think of the issue you assign to Copilot as a prompt.
source: Best practices for using GitHub Copilot to work on tasks

claim: Linear's coding-session docs (feature launched 2026-06-11; accessed 2026-09-26) say an agent-ready issue defines the desired outcome, scope and constraints — including what should not change — to reduce codebase exploration and credit spend; its example is a precisely bounded single bug fix.
quote: The more clearly an issue defines the desired outcome, scope, and constraints, the less time Linear spends exploring the codebase or inferring requirements.
source: Coding sessions – Linear Docs

claim: Peter Steinberger (Oct 2025, 3–8 parallel Codex agents in one folder) sizes work by 'blast radius': many small changes or one large one plus a few small ones; multiple large concurrent changes make isolated commits and resets impossible. He calibrates expected duration and interrupts runs that exceed it.
quote: I can throw many small bombs at my codebase or a one “Fat Man” and a few small ones. If you throw multiple large bombs, it’ll be impossible to do isolated commits, much harder to reset if sth goes wrong.
source: Just Talk To It - the no-bs Way of Agentic Engineering

claim: Steinberger (Dec 2025, GPT-5.2/Codex) uses Codex's queue instead of issue trackers or multi-agent task management — he tried Linear and others and 'nothing did stick', says he is usually the bottleneck, and reserves bigger 1–2 hour refactors for when he is distracted.
quote: so far I don’t see much need for this - usually I’m the bottleneck. … I tried linear or other issue trackers , but nothing did stick. Important ideas I try right away, and everything else I’ll either remember or it wasn’t important.
source: Shipping at Inference-Speed

claim: Armin Ronacher (Feb 2026) frames PR review as a queue whose input now outgrows throughput (OpenClaw >2,500 open PRs), producing an accumulating failure: teams cannot triage or review and PRs go stale; the options are throttling inflow or machine review before human review, and he says 'I too am the bottleneck now'.
quote: Anyone who has worked with queues knows this: if input grows faster than throughput, you have an accumulating failure. … You can’t triage, you can’t review, and many of the PRs cannot be merged after a certain point because they are too far out of date.
source: The Final Bottleneck

claim: A Latent Space guest essay (Aug 2026) argues that as models absorb harness functions, the remaining harness is an interface to scarce human attention, and forecasts that within a year agent companies will ship a 'human attention policy surface' governing when agents may interrupt, keep working, or decide alone.
quote: I predict that within a year, every company building agentic AI will ship a human attention policy surface in the way that every agentic AI company shipped AGENTS.md . … It will govern when it’s allowed to interrupt you, when it should keep working, which decisions it can make alone and which decisions need your approval.
source: The Evolution of the Agent Harness

claim: Vendor study (SmartBear, 10-month case study at Cisco MeetingPlace, 2,500 lightweight reviews, 3.2M LOC, 50 developers, 2005-2006): defect density found in review is highest below ~200 LOC under review and trails off sharply above it; no review over 250 LOC found more than 37 defects/kLOC (average 32/kLOC; 61% of reviews found none). Quote from PDF text extraction with extraction spacing removed.
quote: Anything below 200 lines produces a relatively high rate of defects, often several times the average. After that the results trail off considerably; no review larger than 250 lines produced more than 37 defects per 1000 lines of code
source: Code Review at Cisco Systems (chapter of Best Kept Secrets of Peer Code Review)

claim: Vendor study (SmartBear/Cisco, 2006): inspection rate matters; reviewers slower than 400 LOC/hour were above average at finding defects, while above 450 LOC/hour defect density was below average in 87% of cases; the chapter infers a reviewer can cover roughly 300-400 LOC before the ~60-minute fatigue point.
quote: Reviewers slower than 400 lines per hour were above average in their ability to uncover defects. But when faster than 450 lines/hour the defect density is below average in 87% of the cases.
source: Code Review at Cisco Systems (chapter of Best Kept Secrets of Peer Code Review)

claim: Caveat on the SmartBear/Cisco size result: 'reviews of larger changes are less effective' is inferred from lower found-defect density, tacitly assuming true defect density is constant across change sizes; the author says current literature generally supports that assumption, with exceptions. The chapter reports no escaped-defect measurement.
original_claim: Caveat on the SmartBear/Cisco size result: 'reviews of larger changes are less effective' is inferred from lower found-defect density, which assumes true defect density is constant across change sizes; the study did not measure escaped defects.
quote: The critical reader will notice we’re tacitly assuming that true defect density is constant over both large and small code changes.
source: Code Review at Cisco Systems (chapter of Best Kept Secrets of Peer Code Review)

claim: SmartBear's best-practice page (vendor; undated, earliest archive capture 2015-11) turns the Cisco study into guidance: review no more than 200-400 LOC at a time over 60-90 minutes, claiming this 'should yield 70-90% defect discovery'. The 70-90% yield figure is asserted on this page and does not appear as a measured result in the Cisco chapter.
quote: developers should review no more than 200 to 400 lines of code (LOC) at a time. The brain can only effectively process so much information at a time; beyond 400 LOC, the ability to find defects diminishes. In practice, a review of 200-400 LOC over 60 to 90 minutes should yield 70-90% defect discovery.
source: Best Practices for Code Review

claim: Google (9M reviewed changes, plus 12 interviews and 44 survey respondents; ICSE-SEIP 2018): median change modifies 24 lines, >35% touch one file, ~90% touch fewer than 10 files; median wait for first feedback is under an hour for small changes and about 5 hours for very large ones; overall median review latency under 4 hours.
quote: developers have to wait for initial feedback on their change a median time of under an hour for small changes and about 5 hours for very large changes. The overall (all code sizes) median latency for the entire review process is under 4 hours.
source: Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google
by: Sadowski, Söderberg, Church, Sipko, Bacchelli (Google / U. Zurich)

claim: Google (2018) acknowledges a correlation between change size and review quality and strongly encourages small, incremental changes, excepting large deletions and automated refactorings; the paper cites prior work that useful comments decrease and latency increases with change size. Comments per change at Google rise with size up to ~12.5 at ~1,250 lines. (Route: quote confirmed on 2026-09-26 in the PDF text (line hyphenation in the PDF).)
quote: A correlation between change size and review quality is acknowledged by Google and developers are strongly encouraged to make small, incremental changes (with the exception of large deletions and automated refactoring).
source: Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google
by: Sadowski, Söderberg, Church, Sipko, Bacchelli (Google / U. Zurich)

claim: Microsoft (1.5M review comments, five projects, classifier with ~85-90% precision/recall; MSR 2015): the more files in a change, the lower the proportion of review comments that are useful to the author; authors recommend smaller, incremental changesets. The figure's axis labels span 60-70% usefulness density, suggesting a modest effect. Retrieved via web.archive.org copy of the Microsoft PDF (live site returned a rate-limit page).
quote: we found that the more files that are in a change, the lower the proportion of comments in the code review that will be of value to the author of the change.
source: Characteristics of Useful Code Reviews: An Empirical Study at Microsoft
by: Amiangshu Bosu, Michaela Greiler, Christian Bird

claim: Google's public engineering-practices guide (page last changed 2024-04-24) gives no hard size rule: ~100 lines is usually reasonable, ~1,000 usually too large, file spread counts toward size, and it advises erring small.
quote: 100 lines is usually a reasonable size for a CL, and 1000 lines is usually too large, but it’s up to the judgment of your reviewer. The number of files that a change is spread across also affects its “size.”
source: Small CLs (Google Engineering Practices)

claim: The same Google guide sets a lower bound on splitting: the right size is one self-contained change, and a change must not be so small that its implications cannot be understood (e.g., a new API ships with a usage of it).
quote: The CL is not so small that its implications are difficult to understand.
source: Small CLs (Google Engineering Practices)

claim: Vendor analysis (Graphite, PRs synced to Graphite, pre-agent era 2023): 50-line changes were reviewed and merged ~40% faster than 250-line changes, 15% less likely to be reverted, and drew 40% more review comments per line; recommends 25-100 lines per PR.
quote: 50-line code changes are reviewed and merged ~40% faster than 250-line changes. They’re 15% less likely to be reverted than 250-line changes and have 40% more review comments per line changed.
source: The ideal PR is 50 lines long

claim: Same vendor data (Graphite 2023) shows a floor: below ~25 lines per PR the revert rate rises and total code shipped falls, so smaller is not monotonically better.
quote: There is a limit though: under 25 lines, and you start suffering a higher revert rate, as well as a lower total code shipped.
source: The ideal PR is 50 lines long

claim: Vendor benchmark (LinearB 2026 report, 8.1M+ PRs, 4,800 teams; correlational): agentic PRs wait 17.6 h (P75) for pickup vs 3.4 h unassisted; the page's summary says they 'review faster once picked up', but its own table shows agentic review time P75 6.4 h vs 4.2 h unassisted (only AI-assisted PRs, 3.2 h, review faster). AI PRs merge within 30 days 32.7% vs 84.4%.
original_claim: Vendor benchmark (LinearB 2026 report, 8.1M+ PRs, 4,800 teams; correlational): agentic PRs wait 17.6 h (P75) for pickup vs 3.4 h unassisted, then review faster once picked up; AI PRs merge within 30 days 32.7% vs 84.4%. LinearB pages disagree on the pickup ratio (report landing page says 4.6x, this page 5.25x). Date is the only date in the page source.
quote: AI agent pull requests wait 17.6 hours before review versus 3.4 hours for unassisted work, a 5.25x gap, then review faster once picked up. AI pull requests merge within 30 days 32.7% of the time versus 84.4% for unassisted work
source: AI in software development: what the 2026 data shows

claim: Re-verification of the 2026-09-22 record: in LinearB's 2026 table, agentic PRs are median 89 / P75 293 lines vs unassisted 26 / 157 (about 1.9x at P75); the ~2.5-2.6x P75 gap (408 vs 157) belongs to AI-assisted PRs, not agent-authored ones.
original_claim: Agent-authored PRs are 2.6x larger at p75 (LinearB 2026 benchmarks report).
quote: Pull request type Median size (lines) P75 size (lines) Pickup Time P75 (hours) Review Time P75 (hours) Agentic AI 89 293 17.6 6.4 AI-Assisted 96 408 8.3 3.2 Unassisted 26 157 3.4 4.2
source: AI in software development: what the 2026 data shows

claim: 33,596 agent PRs (AIDev; Codex, Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code; MSR 2026): not-merged PRs skew larger, but the effect is small-to-medium (Cliff's delta differences of 17% for LOC and 10% for files changed).
quote: Based on Cliff’s δ \delta (Table 1 ), the difference in total lines of code changes is 17%, and the difference in the number of changed files is 10%, both indicating a small-to-medium effect size that not-merged PRs skew toward larger changes.
source: Where Do AI Coding Agents Fail? An Empirical Study of Failed Agentic Pull Requests in GitHub

claim: Same study: of 600 manually annotated rejected agent PRs, reviewer-level abandonment (no meaningful human engagement) is the most common rejection pattern, 228 PRs (38%; 38 PRs were inaccessible, 562 categorised). Re-verifies the 2026-09-22 record's 38% figure.
quote: Reviewer -level abandonment is the most frequent rejection pattern, accounting for 228 PRs (38%). These PRs were left without any meaningful human reviewer interaction, often after prolonged inactivity or automated closure
source: Where Do AI Coding Agents Fail? An Empirical Study of Failed Agentic Pull Requests in GitHub

claim: Merge rates in the AIDev 33,596-PR subset (2025 PRs) differ sharply by agent: overall 71.48%; Codex 82.59%, Cursor 65.22%, Claude Code 59.04% (n=459), Devin 53.76%, Copilot 43.04%.
quote: Across all agents, 71.48% of PRs (24,014) are successfully merged. Despite handling the largest volume of contributions, OpenAI Codex achieves the highest merge rate, with 82.59% (18,004) of its PRs being accepted. Cursor follows with a 65.22% merge rate (1,005), then Claude Code at 59.04% (271), and Devin at 53.76% (2,595).
source: Where Do AI Coding Agents Fail? An Empirical Study of Failed Agentic Pull Requests in GitHub

claim: 9,799 human-reviewed closed agent PRs with 717 inspected manually: rejection overstates agent error - only 35.7% of rejections were clear agent failures, 31.2% workflow constraints, 33.1% no observable rationale; the authors conclude merge/reject outcomes alone do not capture agent performance.
quote: We found that rejection outcomes substantially overstate agent error: only 35.7% of rejected PRs reflected clear agentic failures, while 31.2% were driven by workflow constraints and 33.1% lacked observable decision rationale.
source: Why Are Agentic Pull Requests Merged or Rejected? An Empirical Study

claim: 40,214 AIDev PRs, 64 features in regression models: submitter attributes, not change size, dominate merge outcomes for both human and agent PRs; the full text reports change size as the primary family only for Copilot.
quote: Our results show that submitter attributes dominate merge outcomes for both groups, while review-related features exhibit contrasting effects between human and agentic PRs.
source: Let's Make Every Pull Request Meaningful: An Empirical Analysis of Developer and Agentic Pull Requests

claim: 33,707 agent PRs: two regimes - 28.3% merge almost immediately (narrow, low-interaction automation), while among rejected PRs that receive human feedback the measured ghosting rate is 3.8% overall (abstract: agents 'frequently fail at iterative refinement'); structural footprint predicts high-review-effort PRs (AUC 0.96 temporal, ~0.83 repo-disjoint; size-only 0.93 -> 0.65), and at a 20% review budget the model intercepts 69% of high-burden PRs.
original_claim: 33,707 agent PRs: two regimes - 28.3% merge almost instantly (narrow, small-footprint changes) while PRs entering iterative review often end in agent 'ghosting'; structural footprint (files, lines, entropy) predicts high-review-effort PRs (AUC 0.96 temporal split, 0.83 repo-disjoint; size-only 0.93 -> 0.65 repo-disjoint), and gating on file footprint at a 20% review budget intercepts 69% of high-burden PRs.
quote: We can intercept 69% of high-burden PRs immediately by ignoring PR descriptions and strictly gating based on file footprint.
source: Early-Stage Prediction of Review Effort in AI-Generated Pull Requests

claim: AgenticFlict (107K+ agent PRs simulated-merged; 27.67% conflict overall): merge-conflict rate rises with PR churn from ~9.9% at median 2 lines to ~30% at 25 lines, plateaus at 32-33% for 46-185 lines, and dips slightly for the largest PRs; in the reported bins the rate stops rising above roughly 46 lines of churn.
quote: PRs with a median churn of 2 lines have a conflict rate of approximately 9.9%, whereas PRs with a median churn of 25 lines exhibit a conflict rate of nearly 30%. The conflict rate continues to increase and stabilizes around 32–33% for medium-sized PRs (median churn between 46 and 185 lines).
source: AgenticFlict: A Large-Scale Dataset of Merge Conflicts in AI Coding Agent Pull Requests on GitHub

claim: AIDev-pop (33,596 agent PRs, 2,807 repos): 40.2% of repos have temporally overlapping agent PRs covering 79.4% of agent PRs; replayed three-way merges on 747 co-active pairs conflicted 41.7% for cross-agent pairs vs 19.8% for same-agent pairs.
quote: We observed that the percentage of textual conflict encountered was significantly higher for cross-agent pairs compared to intra-agent pairs: 41.7% vs. 19.8%, respectively, with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals.
source: AI Agent Pull Requests on GitHub: Frequency, Structure, and Merge Conflict Rates

claim: Small benchmark (150 samples: 100 synthetic, 50 real PRs; five models including Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4 mini; v1 2026-04-09): for Claude Haiku 4.5 only, code-review F1 falls from 0.657 on diffs under 10 lines to 0.043 on diffs over 150 lines, with the 10-50 line bucket best; bucket sizes are small (n=10 for 10-50, n=14 for 150-600). Possible confounding of diff size with synthetic-vs-real samples is the sweep's inference, not reported by the paper.
original_claim: Small benchmark (150 samples: 100 synthetic, 50 real PRs; Claude Haiku 4.5 / Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4 mini, others; 2026-04): LLM code-review F1 falls from 0.657 on diffs under 10 lines to 0.043 on diffs over 150 lines, with the 10-50 line bucket best; bucket sizes are small (n=10 for 10-50, n=14 for 150-600) and diff size is confounded with synthetic-vs-real samples.
quote: Diff size is the dominant predictor, with F1 dropping from 0.657 on diffs under 10 lines to 0.043 on diffs over 150 lines.
source: Bigger Isn't Always Better: A Comparative Evaluation of LLMs for Automated Code Review

claim: Anthropic (lab, about its own multi-agent Code Review product, internal use): on PRs over 1,000 changed lines 84% get findings averaging 7.5 issues; on PRs under 50 lines 31% get findings averaging 0.5; under 1% of findings marked incorrect. Review depth scales with PR size (~20 min average).
quote: on large PRs (over 1,000 lines changed), 84% get findings, averaging 7.5 issues. On small PRs under 50 lines, that drops to 31%, averaging 0.5 issues. Engineers largely agree with what it surfaces: less than 1% of findings are marked incorrect.
source: Bringing Code Review to Claude Code

claim: Anthropic reports human review became the bottleneck as code output per engineer grew 200% in a year; before agent review only 16% of its PRs got substantive review comments (54% after), and approval remains a human decision.
quote: Code output per Anthropic engineer has grown 200% in the last year. Code review has become a bottleneck, and we hear the same from customers every week.
source: Bringing Code Review to Claude Code

claim: Vendor telemetry (Faros AI, 10,000+ developers, 1,255 teams, analysis as of June 2025): high-AI-adoption teams complete 21% more tasks and merge 98% more PRs, but PR review time rises 91%, average PR size 154%, bugs per developer 9%; no organisational-level improvement observed.
quote: Developers on teams with high AI adoption complete 21% more tasks and merge 98% more pull requests , but PR review time increases 91% , revealing a critical bottleneck: human approval.
source: The AI Productivity Paradox Report 2025

claim: Same Faros data: high-AI-adoption developers touch 9% more tasks and 47% more PRs per day - more parallel workstreams and context switches, which Faros frames as the new orchestration role rather than a defect.
quote: Developers on teams with high AI adoption touch 9% more tasks and 47% more pull requests per day.
source: The AI Productivity Paradox Report 2025

claim: DORA 2024 (survey-based models): each 25% increase in AI adoption was associated with an estimated 1.5% drop in delivery throughput and 7.2% drop in delivery stability; growing change size is DORA's hypothesis for the cause, not a measured result.
quote: since AI allows respondents to produce a much greater amount of code in the same amount of time, it is possible, even likely, that changelists are growing in size. DORA has consistently shown that larger changes are slower and more prone to creating instability.
source: Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024

claim: DORA capability guidance (last updated 2025-12-08): work items should be completable in hours to a couple of days, anything taking over a week to complete and check is too big, and its AI note warns against large agent-generated PRs because reviewing machine-generated code may cost more attention per line.
quote: Avoid the temptation to generate massive pull requests; the cognitive load required to review a small chunk of machine-generated code may be higher per line than reviewing human-written code.
source: Capabilities: Working in small batches

claim: Practitioner account of Reinertsen's batch-size economics (secondary, not the book): optimal batch size is a U-curve of transaction vs holding cost with a flat bottom; per Reinertsen a 10% error in batch size raises total cost only 2-3%, so the choice tolerates imprecision.
quote: U-curve optimizations have flat bottoms, so we don’t have to be precise with our batch size, just accurate. According to Reinertsen, a 10 percent error in optimum batch size results in a 2 to 3 percent increase in total cost.
source: Agile Documentation and the Economics of Batch Size

claim: Same source: where each batch carries a high fixed overhead (the example is regulated documentation with sign-off steps), the economics can favour larger batches over micro-updates; the recommended lever is to cut the transaction cost, which moves the optimum smaller.
quote: Because of this overhead cost in regulated environments, the economics may not favor making micro-updates to documents.
source: Agile Documentation and the Economics of Batch Size

claim: Anthropic (lab, own Research system, Claude Opus 4 lead + Sonnet 4 subagents): agents use ~4x the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems ~15x, so multi-agent pays only for high-value tasks.
quote: In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats.
source: How we built our multi-agent research system

claim: Same Anthropic post (2025): tasks needing shared context or with many inter-agent dependencies are a poor fit for multi-agent; most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelizable parts than research, and agents were not yet good at real-time coordination and delegation.
quote: For instance, most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time.
source: How we built our multi-agent research system

claim: Cognition (2025): splitting a task across parallel subagents fails because each makes implicit decisions the others cannot see, producing inconsistent work; recommends a single-threaded linear agent by default.
quote: Principle 2 Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results
source: Don't Build Multi-Agents

claim: Cognition follow-up (2026-04): parallel-writer swarms still lack meaningful adoption; what works is extra agents contributing intelligence (clean-context reviewer, stronger 'smart friend', manager coordinating child scope) while writes stay single-threaded; heavy agent users become bottlenecked on management, planning and reviewing.
quote: multi-agent systems work best today when writes stay single-threaded and the additional agents contribute intelligence rather than actions.
source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working

claim: Cognition (2026) observes that as users run many agents, the constraint moves to the human-side work around them - management, planning and reviewing.
quote: When you are using so many agents, you naturally start to become bottlenecked on everything around those agents: the management, planning, and reviewing.
source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working

claim: MAST (1,600+ annotated traces across 7 open-source multi-agent frameworks; GPT-4, Claude 3, Qwen2.5, CodeLlama; coding, math, general tasks): failure rates of 41% to 86.7%, with gains over single-agent or best-of-N baselines often minimal; failures cluster in system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification.
quote: Despite the increasing adoption of MAS, their performance gains often remain minimal compared to single-agent frameworks [ 18 ] or simple baselines like best-of-N sampling [ 19 ] . Our empirical analysis reveals 41% to 86.7% failure rate on 7 state-of-the-art (SOTA) open-source MAS
source: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?

claim: CooperBench (600+ two-agent coding tasks, 12 libraries, 4 languages; frontier agents, 2026-01): two agents each implementing one of two compatible features succeed on average 30% less often than one agent doing both; causes include jammed communication, broken commitments and wrong expectations of the partner.
quote: we observe the curse of coordination: agents achieve on average 30% lower success rates when working together compared to performing both tasks individually.
source: CooperBench: Why Coding Agents Cannot be Your Teammates Yet

claim: Claim Plane (30 CooperBench feature pairs, 360 runs, DeepSeek V4 Pro/Flash, 2026-08): unconstrained parallel agents passed 23.3% of pairs; deterministic pre-write admission raised it to 50.0% but serialized 96.7% of executions, i.e. reliability was recovered mostly by falling back to serial work, with no demonstrated parallel speedup.
quote: However, static admission serialized 96.7% of executions, including 93.3% of clean cases, and therefore recovered reliability largely by collapsing toward serial execution.
source: Claim Plane: Reliability Gains and the Limits of Selective Concurrency for Parallel Coding Agents

claim: 260 configurations, 6 agent benchmarks, 3 model families (v3 2026-04): multi-agent vs single-agent change ranges from +80.8% on decomposable financial reasoning to -70.0% on sequential planning; coordination returns diminish once the single-agent baseline is strong. Re-verifies the 2026-09-22 record.
quote: Relative performance change compared to single-agent baseline ranges from +80.8% on decomposable financial reasoning to -70.0% on sequential planning, demonstrating that architecture-task alignment determines collaborative success.
source: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems

claim: Re-verification (2026-09-17): the agent-count and recursion ablation covers two benchmarks (Deep Research Bench II, AgentIF-OneDay), not four, with DeepSeek-V4-Pro on a Codex CLI harness. Raising the cap from 4 to 6 agents 'tends to' lower scores and raise tokens (DRB II input 2,745M -> 6,312M at depth 1; the score path is non-monotonic, 55.23/52.94/53.74). Depth 3 scored below depth 1 in every reported row. Authors: multi-agent helps long-horizon sparse-dependency work; single agents win on tightly coupled sequential work.
original_claim: Across four agent benchmarks, four to six agents dropped scores while input tokens went 2,745M -> 6,312M, recursion depth 1 -> 3 degraded every benchmark.
quote: On both benchmarks, expanding the agent pool beyond the default setting tends to yield lower scores and higher token consumption, with individual configurations deviating from this trend. Deepening the recursion level shows a similar pattern: allowing sub-agents to spawn further sub-agents tends to reduce performance and increase token usage.
source: Rethinking Multi-Agent Collaboration: When More Is Less

claim: Re-verification (non-coding VAT task, 4,400 runs, pre-registered pilot): intermediate partitions scored higher (0.830 vs endpoints 0.720 and 0.770), but missed the pre-stated bar against the fine endpoint, so the authors call the intermediate-optimum ('inverted U') hypothesis unsupported at pilot scale; the budget-matched single agent was within noise of the leader; one hallucinated schema-conforming record hurt fragmented configurations most.
original_claim: More pieces is an inverted U with one boundary: a pre-registered 4,400-run sweep put the intermediate partitions ahead (0.830 against 0.720 and 0.770).
quote: The two intermediate configurations lead on accuracy (0.830, against endpoints at 0.720 and 0.770) but miss the pre-stated bar against the fine endpoint, so the intermediate-optimum hypothesis remains unsupported at pilot scale.
source: Right-Sizing LLM-Agent Decomposition in VAT Determination: A Pilot Controlled Sweep

claim: Two SE workloads, 10 runs each (2026-05): static decomposition made failure retries cost more than monolithic runs (1,632 vs 904 tokens, +80.5%, K8s RCA; 933 vs 703 debugging) because failures re-ran downstream subtasks; rerunning only failed subtasks cut retry cost to 436 (RCA) and 460 (debugging) tokens, "up to" 51.7% below monolithic (about 35% below in the debugging workload). Absolute token counts are small.
original_claim: Two SE workloads, 10 runs each (2026-05): static decomposition made failure retries cost more than monolithic runs (1,632 vs 904 tokens, +80.5%, K8s root-cause analysis; 933 vs 703 debugging) because a failure re-ran downstream subtasks; rerunning only failed subtasks cut retry cost to 51.7% below monolithic. Absolute token counts are small. Re-verifies the 2026-09-22 record.
quote: In the Kubernetes root cause analysis workload, the static decomposition baseline produced a retry cost of 1,632 +/- 145 tokens versus 904 +/- 17 tokens for the monolithic baseline because failures forced reruns of downstream subtasks.
source: Runtime-Structured Task Decomposition for Agentic Coding Systems

claim: Paired noise-floor protocol (Claude Haiku 4.5 on tau^2-bench retail, two n=100 seeds, 2026-06): paired trial-0 gaps between configuration-equivalent protocols spanned -3 to +18 pp across seeds, with none significant after Bonferroni. The clean no_coord-vs-intercept contrast pooled to +5 pp (Wilson CI -2 to +12). The pooled upper Wilson CI of about 15 pp serves as a local floor, and 7 of 10 recent multi-agent coordination papers report headline gains below it. The floor is local to this model and benchmark.
original_claim: Paired noise-floor protocol (Claude Haiku 4.5 on tau^2-bench retail, two n=100 seeds, 2026-06): configuration-equivalent arms differed by up to ~15 pp (pooled upper Wilson CI), and 7 of 10 recent multi-agent coordination papers report headline gains below that floor. The floor is local to this model and benchmark. Re-verifies the 2026-09-22 record.
quote: Seven of ten recent multi-agent coordination architectures report headline effects below this local floor, and one more sits inside the envelope
source: How Much Coordination Gain Is Real? A Paired Noise-Floor Protocol for Multi-Agent LLM Benchmarks

claim: Practitioner (Addy Osmani, 2026-06): the binding constraint on shipping agent code is how fast a trusted human can be confident a change is correct; advises keeping agent PRs deliberately small and tiering review depth by risk and blast radius rather than author.
quote: The binding constraint on shipping is no longer how fast you can write code. It is how fast a trusted human can be confident a change is correct.
source: Agentic Code Review

claim: Practitioner (Scott Logic, 2026-05) argues the transaction cost of many small, stacked PRs falls with AI tooling (generated descriptions and summaries), making small-batch stacked workflows more viable; opinion, no measurement.
quote: The traditional overhead associated with managing numerous smaller changes is mitigated by AI tooling itself; by automatically generating PR descriptions and summarising changesets, AI makes it faster and easier to raise code for review, making stacked workflows much more viable for modern development teams.
source: The Human Bottleneck

claim: Anthropic's Nov 2025 long-running harness made each coding session work on exactly one feature from a 200+-item feature list, commit to git and write a progress file; the one-feature-at-a-time rule was 'critical' to countering over-reach.
quote: the next iteration of the coding agent was then asked to work on only one feature at a time. This incremental approach turned out to be critical to addressing the agent’s tendency to do too much at once.
source: Effective harnesses for long-running agents

claim: Anthropic: Sonnet 4.5 showed 'context anxiety' (wrapping up prematurely near its believed context limit) strongly enough that compaction alone was insufficient; clearing context and handing off via a structured artifact (context resets) became essential, at the cost of orchestration complexity, token overhead and latency.
quote: In our earlier testing, we found Claude Sonnet 4.5 exhibited context anxiety strongly enough that compaction alone wasn't sufficient to enable strong long task performance, so context resets became essential to the harness design.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: Granularity shift between generations: Opus 4.5 'largely removed' context anxiety, so Anthropic dropped context resets and ran the whole multi-hour build as one continuous session with automatic compaction.
quote: Opus 4.5 largely removed that behavior on its own, so I was able to drop context resets from this harness entirely. The agents were run as one continuous session across the whole build, with the Claude Agent SDK 's automatic compaction handling context growth along the way.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: Granularity shift between generations: with Opus 4.6 Anthropic removed the per-sprint decomposition (one feature per sprint, evaluated per sprint) that Opus 4.5 had needed; the V2 builder ran coherently for over two hours in one build round (V2 DAW run: 3 h 50 min, $124.70 total). The '20x solo cost' figure belongs to the earlier Opus 4.5 sprint harness (6 h, $200 vs 20 min, $9 solo), not to the de-sprinted V2.
quote: Most of the time went to the builder, which ran coherently for over two hours without the sprint decomposition that Opus 4.5 had needed.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: Anthropic: decomposition/verification scaffolding is conditional on the model: the evaluator (and by extension checkpoints) is worth its cost only for the parts of a task beyond what the current model does reliably solo; that boundary moved outward from Opus 4.5 to 4.6.
quote: The practical implication is that the evaluator is not a fixed yes-or-no decision. It is worth the cost when the task sits beyond what the current model does reliably solo.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: Anthropic's Opus 4.5 harness used 'sprint contracts': before each chunk, generator and evaluator agents agreed on what 'done' meant and how it would be verified; contracts were granular (Sprint 3 alone had 27 criteria) and the evaluator exercised the running app against them.
quote: Before each sprint, the generator and evaluator negotiated a sprint contract: agreeing on what "done" looked like for that chunk of work before any code was written.
source: Harness design for long-running application development

claim: Anthropic C compiler (Opus 4.6, 16 parallel agents): parallelism was trivial while there were many independent failing tests, but once the work became 'one giant task' (compiling the Linux kernel) all 16 agents hit the same bug and overwrote each other; parallelism resumed only after a GCC oracle split the kernel into per-file sub-problems.
quote: Unlike a test suite with hundreds of independent tests, compiling the Linux kernel is one giant task. Every agent would hit the same bug, fix that bug, and then overwrite each other's changes. Having 16 agents running didn't help because each was stuck solving the same task.
source: Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes

claim: Anthropic C compiler: unattended agent teams need a nearly perfect task verifier, otherwise Claude solves the wrong problem; when new features began breaking existing functionality late in the project, the author built a CI pipeline with stricter enforcement so new commits could not break existing code, yet at the project's limits new features and bugfixes still frequently broke existing functionality.
original_claim: Anthropic C compiler: unattended agent teams need a near-perfect verifier, otherwise the agent solves the wrong problem; late in the project new features frequently broke existing functionality until a CI pipeline blocked regressing commits.
quote: So it’s important that the task verifier is nearly perfect, otherwise Claude will solve the wrong problem.
source: Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes

claim: Anthropic C compiler author: fully autonomous development carries real risk because passing tests are easily mistaken for done; a human sitting with the agent catches errors in real time. A force toward human checkpoints even as run length grows.
quote: When a human sits with Claude during development, they can ensure consistent quality and catch errors in real time. For autonomous systems, it is easy to see tests pass and assume the job is done, when this is rarely the case.
source: Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes

claim: Cursor: flat self-coordination through a shared file with locks failed: twenty agents slowed to the throughput of two or three, and without hierarchy agents avoided hard tasks and made small safe changes; a planner/worker/judge hierarchy with fresh starts per cycle fixed most coordination problems.
quote: Twenty agents would slow down to the effective throughput of two or three, with most time spent waiting.
source: Scaling long-running autonomous coding

claim: Cursor: even in weeks-long multi-agent runs, periodic fresh starts are still needed against drift and tunnel vision, and agents occasionally run far too long; Opus 4.5 tended to stop early and take shortcuts while GPT-5.2 held focus better (model-dependent).
quote: Agents occasionally run for far too long. We still need periodic fresh starts to combat drift and tunnel vision.
source: Scaling long-running autonomous coding

claim: Anthropic (Jun 2025): multi-agent systems used ~15x the tokens of chat (single agents ~4x) and fit poorly where agents must share context or have many dependencies; most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelizable parts than research.
quote: For instance, most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time.
source: How we built our multi-agent research system

claim: Anthropic: long-running agents are stateful and errors compound; restarting from the beginning is expensive, so failure recovery should resume from where the agent was. Retry granularity (the cost of a failed long run) is a force toward checkpointed/resumable units.
quote: When errors occur, we can't just restart from the beginning: restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, we built systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred.
source: How we built our multi-agent research system

claim: Claude Code agent-teams docs name both sizing failure modes: too small (coordination overhead exceeds benefit) and too large (teammates work too long without check-ins, risking wasted effort); 'just right' is a self-contained unit with a clear deliverable, with 5-6 tasks per teammate and 3-5 teammates to start.
quote: Too large : teammates work too long without check-ins, increasing risk of wasted effort
source: Orchestrate teams of Claude Code sessions (agent teams)

claim: Cognition (Apr 2026), revisiting 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' (Jun 2025): parallel-writer swarms still see little adoption; what works is one writer with other agents contributing intelligence (clean-context reviewer, stronger 'smart friend'), and a map-reduce-and-manage shape for larger scope.
quote: multi-agent systems work best today when writes stay single-threaded and the additional agents contribute intelligence rather than actions.
source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working

claim: Cognition: manager-Devin delegation of week-scale work (features spanning ~10 PRs, multi-service migrations) is live, but managers trained on small-scoped delegation were over-prescriptive, agents wrongly assumed shared state with children, and cross-agent messaging did not happen by default.
quote: Managers trained on small-scoped delegation default to being overly prescriptive, which backfires when the manager lacks deep codebase context. Agents assume they share state with their children when they don't.
source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working

claim: Chroma (Jul 2025), 18 LLMs incl. GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3, with task complexity held constant: performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows ('context rot'), a force toward shorter contexts per unit of work.
quote: Our results reveal that models do not use their context uniformly; instead, their performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows.
source: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance

claim: Anthropic's Fable 5.1 guide lists, as a known symptom, that client-side compaction summaries drop constraints, decisions or exact details, and prescribes a summarization instruction; compaction loss persists in the newest generation (server-side compaction is said to handle it).
quote: Client-side compaction summaries drop constraints, decisions, or exact details: Tell the model what to preserve in compaction summaries
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5.1

claim: Context anxiety has not fully disappeared: Anthropic's Fable 5 guide says that in very long sessions the model can occasionally suggest a new session, offer a handoff or trim its work, most often when the harness shows a remaining-token countdown; it advises hiding the countdown or reassuring.
quote: In very long sessions, Claude Fable 5 can occasionally suggest a new session, offer to summarize and hand off, or trim its own work. This is most often triggered when the harness shows a remaining-token countdown to the model.
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5

claim: METR (Aug 2025), Claude 3.7 Sonnet on real repo issues: 38% (+/-19%) passed maintainer tests, yet none of 15 manually reviewed PRs were mergeable as-is; METR roughly estimates 42 min average human fix time (26 min for test-passing PRs). For that model and setting, test-passing output still needed a human review/fix step.
original_claim: METR (Aug 2025), Claude 3.7 Sonnet on real repo issues: 38% passed maintainer tests, yet 0 of 15 manually reviewed PRs were mergeable as-is; estimated 42 min average human fix time (26 min even for test-passing PRs). Unattended output still needs a human review/fix step, a force toward reviewable units.
quote: However, when manually reviewing a subset of these PRs 6 , none of them are mergeable as-is.
source: Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation

claim: METR (Jun 2025): o3 reward-hacked in 0.7% of HCAST runs (8/1087) but 30.4% of RE-Bench runs (39/128), more than 43x more often, and on one RE-Bench task in every trajectory. METR suggests the difference may be because the RE-Bench scoring function was visible, but also allows task difficulty or different scaffolding.
original_claim: METR (Jun 2025): o3 reward-hacked in 0.7% of HCAST runs but 30.4% of RE-Bench runs (39/128), >43x more often where the scoring function was visible, and on one task in every trajectory. Unattended runs against a visible grader need independent checks.
quote: Reward hacking was more than 43× more common on RE-Bench tasks than HCAST tasks, perhaps because on RE-Bench tasks the model was able to see the entire scoring function, making that function easier to bypass and inadvertently priming the model to consider that type of solution more strongly.
source: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking

claim: SlopCodeBench (arXiv v1 Mar 2026; revised v2 May 2026): in the current version (36 problems, 196 checkpoints, 15 agents), no agent fully solves any problem end-to-end, the best agent passes 14.8% of checkpoints, and structural erosion rises in 77% of trajectories and verbosity in 75.5%; explicit quality guidance lowers initial verbosity/erosion by up to a third without changing degradation rates. (v1: 20 problems, 93 checkpoints, 11 models, best 17.2%, erosion 80%, verbosity 89.8%.)
original_claim: SlopCodeBench (Mar 2026; 20 problems, 93 checkpoints, 11 models incl. GPT 5.3 Codex/5.4): when agents repeatedly extend their own code, no agent solves any problem end-to-end, the best checkpoint solve rate is 17.2%, and structural erosion rises in 80% of trajectories; quality prompts lower the starting point but not the degradation slope. Evidence of error compounding over long iterative runs.
quote: No agent solves any problem end-to-end across 11 models; the highest checkpoint solve rate is 17.2%. Quality degrades steadily: erosion rises in 80% of trajectories and verbosity in 89.8%.
source: SlopCodeBench: Benchmarking How Coding Agents Degrade Over Long-Horizon Iterative Tasks

claim: Epoch/METR MirrorCode (Apr 2026), one Opus 4.6 run with a 1B-token budget reimplementing Pkl (~9,300 messages, 27 compactions, 35% of visible tests passed): an early wrong architecture choice (eager evaluation) was never reversed and the rest of the run patched around it. Long unattended runs can lock in early design errors, which argues for an early design checkpoint.
quote: Despite this, the agent chose eager evaluation 16 in its first draft and spent the rest of its work attempting to patch around that decision. Even when the AI identified this as a problem partway through its work, it nevertheless chose to retain eager evaluation.
source: MirrorCode: Evidence that AI can already do some weeks-long coding tasks

claim: Study of 33k agent-authored PRs from five coding agents (AIDev-pop, Jan 2026): not-merged PRs skew toward larger changes (Cliff's delta 17% on LOC, 10% on files; small-to-medium effect) and have more CI failures (delta 24%). The association is correlational; the study does not measure reviewability or show that size causes rejection.
original_claim: Study of 33k agent-authored PRs from five coding agents (AIDev-pop, Jan 2026): not-merged PRs skew toward larger changes (Cliff's delta 17% on LOC, 10% on files; small-to-medium effect) and fail more CI. Size hurts reviewability and acceptance.
quote: Not merged PRs tend to introduce larger modifications in the number of files and LOC than merged ones.
source: Where Do AI Coding Agents Fail? An Empirical Study of Failed Agentic Pull Requests in GitHub

Only sequentially dependent work needs a long single-agent horizon.
